DLEC-CTX-G2.title: CS 261 Lecture 11 notes - Binary heaps and build-heap
DLEC-CTX-G2.text:
CS 261 - Data Structures
Lecture 11 Notes: Binary Heaps and Build-Heap
Prof. Tomasz Reinholt-Vega | Carrow Institute of Technology

1. What a binary heap is
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array that satisfies the heap-order property. In CS 261 we use MIN-heaps by default: every node's key is less than or equal to the keys of its children, so the smallest key sits at the root.

2. CS 261 array convention (differs from the 0-indexed code you will see online)
We store the heap 1-indexed. Index 0 is left empty (we write it as _).
- parent(i) = floor(i / 2)
- left(i) = 2i
- right(i) = 2i + 1
If you see parent(i) = floor((i - 1) / 2) and left(i) = 2i + 1 online, that is the 0-indexed layout. Both are correct for their own layout, but on CS 261 quizzes you must use the 1-indexed formulas.

3. Height convention
In CS 261 the height of a tree counts NODES on the longest root-to-leaf path, so a single node has height 1 and an empty tree has height 0. (Most textbooks count edges, so for them a single node has height 0.) With our convention a heap with n keys has height floor(log2 n) + 1. Example: n = 7 gives height 3.

4. Sift-down (heapify at index i)
Compare the key at i with its children. If the smaller child is smaller than the key at i, swap with that smaller child and repeat from the child's index. Stop when the key is no larger than both children or when i has no children. Cost: O(height).

5. Build-heap (bottom-up)
Call sift-down on i = floor(n / 2), floor(n / 2) - 1, ..., 1. Leaves (indices greater than floor(n / 2)) are already heaps, so we skip them.
Total cost is O(n), not O(n log n). Most nodes live near the bottom and can only sift down a short distance; the sum of heights over all nodes is bounded by a linear function of n.

6. Worked example (show the array after every sift-down call; this is required on quizzes)
Input, n = 7: [_, 9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6]
Start at i = floor(7 / 2) = 3.
- sift-down(3): 7 vs children 2 (i=6) and 6 (i=7). Swap with 2. Array: [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(2): 4 vs children 1 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 1. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(1): 9 vs children 1 (i=2) and 2 (i=3). Swap with 1. Continue at i=2: 9 vs children 4 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 4. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]
Result: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

7. Other operations
- peek-min: O(1), it is A[1].
- insert: put the key at A[n + 1], then sift-up. O(log n).
- extract-min: move A[n] to A[1], shrink the heap, sift-down(1). O(log n).
- Finding the MAXIMUM in a min-heap is not cheap: the max is somewhere among the leaves, so it takes O(n) in general.

8. Logistics
Quiz 4 (next Thursday) covers heaps: sift-down traces, build-heap traces, and the index formulas above. Traces must use the 1-indexed layout. Priority queues and heapsort are on Quiz 5, not Quiz 4.

DLEC-CTX-I1.title: Rennick Library group study room policy
DLEC-CTX-I1.text:
Rennick Library - Group Study Room Policy (Fall Term)

Group study rooms on floors 2 and 3 of Rennick Library can be reserved by current students through the library booking portal. Each room holds between four and eight people and has a wall-mounted display and a whiteboard.

Booking rules
- Reservations open seven days in advance at 8:00 am.
- Each student may hold up to two hours of bookings per day and six hours per week.
- A room is released to the waitlist if nobody from the group checks in at the front desk within 15 minutes of the start time.
- Rooms 3B and 3C are quiet rooms: whiteboard work only, no calls or video meetings.

During exam weeks
- The daily limit drops to 90 minutes so more groups get a turn.
- Overnight booking between midnight and 7:00 am is available only on floor 2.

Care of rooms
- Wipe the whiteboard and take your rubbish with you when you leave.
- Food is not allowed; covered drinks are fine.
- Report broken displays or dried-out markers at the front desk or through the portal's "Report a problem" link.

Repeated no-shows (three in one term) suspend booking privileges for two weeks. Questions: ask at the Rennick front desk or contact the circulation team through the library website.

DLEC-CTX-G1.title: ECON 214 Week 6 slides - Price elasticity of demand
DLEC-CTX-G1.text:
ECON 214 - Intermediate Microeconomics
Week 6 Lecture Slides: Price Elasticity of Demand
Prof. Adaeze Okonkwo-Hale | Harlow State University | Section 002

Slide 1 - Learning goals
- Compute own-price elasticity of demand using the course's midpoint convention
- Classify demand as elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic
- Connect elasticity to what happens to total revenue when price changes

Slide 2 - Definition
Own-price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in the good's own price:
E = (% change in quantity demanded) / (% change in price)
Because demand slopes down, the raw ratio is negative.

Slide 3 - ECON 214 convention (read this carefully)
In this course we ALWAYS use the midpoint (arc) formula unless a question explicitly says "point elasticity":
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / ((Q1 + Q2) / 2)
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / ((P1 + P2) / 2)
We report own-price elasticity as an absolute value, rounded to two decimals. So you write 1.22, not -1.22.
Many textbooks (including the optional Marchetti text) divide by the starting values instead. That gives a different number for the same data, and it gives a different number depending on whether the price goes up or down. The midpoint version gives the same answer in both directions, which is why we use it.

Slide 4 - Classification (using the absolute value |E|)
- |E| > 1: elastic
- |E| < 1: inelastic
- |E| = 1 exactly: unit elastic
Note: 1.00 after rounding counts as unit elastic on problem sets and exams.

Slide 5 - Worked example: the Quad coffee cart
The coffee cart outside Benning Hall raises the price of a small drip coffee from $3.00 to $3.60. Daily sales fall from 500 cups to 400 cups.
Step 1: % change in Q = (400 - 500) / 450 = -0.2222, i.e. -22.2%
Step 2: % change in P = (3.60 - 3.00) / 3.30 = 0.1818, i.e. 18.2%
Step 3: E = -22.2% / 18.2% = -1.22
Step 4: report |E| = 1.22, so demand is elastic over this range.
Check: with the starting-value method you would get -20% / 20% = -1.00 and call it unit elastic. Same data, different classification. This is exactly why we fix one convention.

Slide 6 - Elasticity and total revenue
Total revenue TR = P x Q.
Before: $3.00 x 500 = $1,500 per day. After: $3.60 x 400 = $1,440 per day.
Rule: when demand is elastic, a price increase lowers total revenue; when demand is inelastic, a price increase raises total revenue; at unit elasticity total revenue does not change.
The coffee cart is consistent with the rule: elastic demand, price went up, revenue fell by $60 a day.

Slide 7 - What makes demand more elastic?
- Close substitutes are available (the dining hall sells drip coffee for $2.25)
- The good is a larger share of the budget
- A longer time horizon to adjust
- A narrowly defined market ("drip coffee at this cart" versus "caffeine")

Slide 8 - Exam notes
- Midterm 2 covers Weeks 5 to 8. Elasticity questions on Midterm 2 must use the midpoint formula; answers that use starting values get at most half credit.
- Show all four steps from Slide 5.
- The elasticity formula sheet is NOT provided on Midterm 2. Memorize the formulas.

Slide 9 - Preview of Week 7
Cross-price elasticity: the sign matters there (positive means substitutes, negative means complements), so we do NOT take absolute values for cross-price elasticity.

items.question: another one, different numbers
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): teach me build-heap properly using his worked example: why we start at floor(n/2), what each sift-down does to the array, and why the whole thing is O(n) and not O(n log n).

NATIVELY: Start at floor(n/2) because everything past it is a leaf, and a single node is already a valid heap. So the last node with children is floor(n/2), and you fix heaps bottom-up from there.

In the example, n=7, so you start at i=3. Sift-down(3) swaps 7 with its smaller child 2, giving [_,9,4,2,1,8,7,6]. Sift-down(2) swaps 4 with 1, giving [_,9,1,2,4,8,7,6]. Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then 9 with 4, giving [_,1,4,2,9,8,7,6]. Four swaps.

It's O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only fall a short distance. Summing each node's height gives a linear bound.
USER (typed to Natively): simpler please

NATIVELY: Start at floor(n/2) because everything after that index is a leaf, and a leaf is already a valid heap on its own. So floor(n/2) is the last node that actually has children, and you fix heaps from there back up to the root.

In the example n=7, so you start at i=3. Sift-down(3) swaps 7 with its smaller child 2, giving [_,9,4,2,1,8,7,6]. Sift-down(2) swaps 4 with 1, giving [_,9,1,2,4,8,7,6]. Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then 9 with 4, giving [_,1,4,2,9,8,7,6]. Four swaps total.

It's O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only fall a short distance. Add up each node's height and the total comes out linear in n.
items.answer:
Same idea, fresh numbers. Take n=6, array [_, 5, 3, 8, 1, 9, 2] (1-indexed, ignoring index 0).

floor(n/2) = 3, so you start at i=3 and work back to the root. Everything past index 3 is a leaf, already a valid heap.

Sift-down(3): node 8, children 9 and 2. Swap with the smaller child 2, giving [_, 5, 3, 2, 1, 9, 8].

Sift-down(2): node 3, children 1 and 9. Swap with 1, giving [_, 5, 1, 2, 3, 9, 8].

Sift-down(1): node 5, children 1 and 2. Swap with 1, giving [_, 1, 5, 2, 3, 9, 8]. Now 5 sits at index 2, children 3 and 9, so swap with 3, giving [_, 1, 3, 2, 5, 9, 8]. That's a valid min-heap.

Four swaps again. It's O(n) because most nodes are near the bottom and can only fall a short way, so summing each node's height stays linear in n.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: And this is why industry loves catalysts, right? You add a catalyst to the contact process and it pushes the equilibrium over toward sulfur trioxide, so you end up with a higher yield.
items.answer:
That's a common mix-up, and it's worth correcting. A catalyst speeds up the rate at which the reaction reaches equilibrium, but it doesn't shift the position of equilibrium. It lowers the activation energy for both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the equilibrium constant stays the same and the final yield is unchanged. What a catalyst does buy you is time: equilibrium is reached faster, which matters a lot in industry.

In the contact process, the yield of sulfur trioxide is actually pushed up by other things, like using excess oxygen, removing the SO3 as it forms, and choosing conditions that favor the forward reaction. The catalyst, typically vanadium pentoxide, is there to get you to that equilibrium quickly rather than to move it.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: So in the trial the p-value came out at 0.03, and what that tells us is there's only a three percent chance the null hypothesis is true.
items.answer:
That's actually the most common misreading of a p-value. A p-value of 0.03 means that **if the null hypothesis were true**, you'd see data at least this extreme about three percent of the time. It's the probability of the data given the null, not the probability of the null given the data.

To get the chance the null is true, you'd need a Bayesian posterior, which also depends on your prior. So the correct statement is: the result is unlikely under the null, which is evidence against it, but it doesn't hand you a three percent probability that the null holds.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: And the printing press is the key here, Gutenberg's from around 1450, which is why Luther's Ninety-five Theses in 1517 spread across the German lands in a matter of weeks.
items.answer: Gutenberg's press around 1450 is what made that speed possible. Before movable type, texts were copied by hand, so a single document took months to reproduce. With printing, thousands of copies of the Ninety-five Theses could be run off quickly and carried across the German lands, which is why it spread in weeks rather than years.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: she wrote upside-down A x, backwards E y, Loves(x, y) on the board, then wrote backwards E y, upside-down A x, Loves(x, y) and said they mean totally different things. what are those symbols, how do I read them out loud, and why does swapping the order change the meaning?
items.answer:
The upside-down A is the **universal quantifier**, read "for all." The backwards E is the **existential quantifier**, read "there exists." So the first one reads "for all x, there exists a y such that Loves(x, y)," and the second reads "there exists a y such that for all x, Loves(x, y)."

The order matters because each quantifier's scope extends over everything after it. The first says everyone loves someone, possibly a different person each. The second says there's one single person whom everyone loves. Same symbols, same predicate, completely different claim.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: And that's why the firm's short-run supply curve is just its marginal cost curve, but only the part above the minimum of AVC.
conversation: PROFESSOR: Remember from Tuesday, marginal cost is what it costs to make one more unit, and the MC curve crosses average variable cost at its minimum.
PROFESSOR: And the shutdown rule: in the short run a firm keeps producing as long as price covers average variable cost, not average total cost. Fixed costs are sunk either way.
PROFESSOR: Okay, let's draw the firm's cost curves again.
items.answer: The short-run supply curve is the marginal cost curve above the minimum of average variable cost. The reason is the shutdown rule: a firm produces only when price is at least AVC, so below that minimum it shuts down and supplies nothing. Above it, each extra unit costs MC, so the firm supplies up to the point where price equals MC. That's why the supply curve starts at the bottom of the AVC curve and follows MC upward from there.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: ok so what does it solve to, and show me how you get there
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): she wrote T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) for merge sort and I have no idea how to read that

NATIVELY: That's a **recurrence relation**, a way of writing how long a recursive algorithm takes in terms of itself. Read it as: to sort n items, merge sort splits them into two halves, recursively sorts each half, and then merges the two sorted halves back together.

So **T(n)** is the total time for n items. The **2T(n/2)** part says two subproblems, each half the size. The **Theta(n)** part is the merge step, which takes time proportional to n because you walk through all n elements once. The base case, when you get down to a single element, is constant time.

To solve it, you can use the master theorem: a = 2, b = 2, and the merge cost is n, so you get **Theta(n log n)**. Intuitively, there are log n levels of splitting, and each level does about n work total.
USER (typed to Natively): why n/2?

NATIVELY: The **n/2** is the size of each subproblem. Merge sort splits the array into two halves, so if the whole thing has n items, each half has n/2. The **2** in front is the count: two of those halves. So 2T(n/2) means "two recursive calls, each on half the data."

The Theta(n) is separate, it's the merge step that runs once per level over all n items. Put together, the recursion branches into two halves each time, which is why the total comes out to Theta(n log n).
items.answer:
To solve it, you want the closed form: **T(n) = Theta(n log n)**. Here's how you get there.

The recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n). Match it to the master theorem form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n). Here a = 2, b = 2, and f(n) = Theta(n). Compute log base b of a, which is log base 2 of 2, so that's 1. So n raised to that power is n^1 = n. Since f(n) = Theta(n) matches n^1, you're in the balanced case, and the answer is Theta(n log n).

The intuition: each level of the recursion does about n work total, and the array keeps halving until you hit single elements, which takes log n levels. So n work times log n levels gives Theta(n log n).

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Which means we're basically 97 percent sure the drug works.
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): So in the trial the p-value came out at 0.03, and what that tells us is there's only a three percent chance the null hypothesis is true.

NATIVELY: That's actually the most common misreading of a p-value. A p-value of 0.03 means that **if the null hypothesis were true**, you'd see data at least this extreme about three percent of the time. It's the probability of the data given the null, not the probability of the null given the data.

To get the chance the null is true, you'd need a Bayesian posterior, which also depends on your prior. So the correct statement is: the result is unlikely under the null, which is evidence against it, but it doesn't hand you a three percent probability that the null holds.
items.answer: No, that's the same inversion again. A p-value of 0.03 doesn't give you a 97 percent chance the drug works. It says that if the drug did nothing, data this extreme would show up about three percent of the time. The probability the drug works is a different quantity, and you can't get it by subtracting from one. That needs a Bayesian posterior, which depends on your prior.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: what did she mean by 'the corridor is really just a floor'?
conversation: PROFESSOR: The Fed doesn't really set 'the interest rate.' It sets a target range for the federal funds rate.
PROFESSOR: Back when reserves were scarce, it hit that target with open market operations, buying and selling securities pretty much every day.
PROFESSOR: Now we're in an ample reserves regime, so the main tool is the interest rate on reserve balances, and honestly the corridor is really just a floor.
items.answer: She means the "corridor" isn't a symmetric band anymore. In an ample reserves system, the interest on reserve balances acts as the floor, since banks won't lend below what they can earn at the Fed. The effective rate sits just above it, so the ceiling side barely binds.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: given my background, which parts of today's lecture on SQL joins can I safely skip?
items.answer:
I can't tell you which parts to skip, because nothing here tells me what your background actually covers. What I can do is give you a quick self-check, since joins are one of those topics where the gaps are usually specific rather than general.

If you can already write an inner join from memory and explain why a left join keeps unmatched rows from the left table, the basic syntax and the inner-join section are probably safe to skim. The parts worth staying awake for are the ones people get subtly wrong: the difference between `ON` and `WHERE` in an outer join, what happens when you join on a non-unique key and rows multiply, and how `NULL` behaves in join conditions, since `NULL = NULL` is never true.

So the honest answer is that I'd need to know which of those you've already got solid. If you've used joins regularly in real queries, skip the syntax and sit through the edge cases. If your exposure is mostly textbook, don't skip anything yet.

items.question: whats entropy
items.answer:
Entropy is a measure of how many ways a system can be arranged without changing how it looks from the outside. In thermodynamics it's often described as disorder, but the cleaner idea is missing information: the more arrangements that give the same macroscopic state, the higher the entropy.

A simple example is a shuffled deck of cards. There's essentially one way to have it perfectly ordered, but an enormous number of ways to have it mixed, so a random shuffle has high entropy. The second law says entropy in a closed system tends to increase, which is really just saying systems drift toward their most probable arrangements.

In information theory, Shannon entropy measures the average uncertainty in a message, and it uses the same underlying math.

items.question: Le Chatelier's principle: if you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts in the direction that partly undoes the disturbance.
items.answer: Le Chatelier's principle says a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by shifting in the direction that partially counteracts it. So if you add more reactant, the reaction shifts toward products to use it up. If you increase pressure by shrinking the volume, it shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules. And if you raise the temperature, it shifts in the endothermic direction, the one that absorbs the added heat. The key word is "partly": the shift opposes the change but doesn't fully cancel it, so the system settles at a new equilibrium rather than returning to the old one.

items.question: So to pull it together: long-term you've got the alliance system, militarism, nationalism and imperialism, and then the short-term trigger is Sarajevo and the July Crisis. Next week we'll look at why the war didn't end by Christmas like everyone expected it to.
conversation: PROFESSOR: So Franz Ferdinand is shot in Sarajevo on June 28th, 1914, and for about a month nothing much seems to happen.
PROFESSOR: Then the July Crisis. Germany gives Austria-Hungary what historians call the blank cheque, unconditional support for whatever Vienna does to Serbia.
PROFESSOR: Austria sends an ultimatum it basically expects Serbia to reject, Russia starts mobilizing, and the German war plan needs to go through Belgium, which brings Britain in.
items.answer: The lecturer is wrapping up, so the useful thing is a clean summary of the causes. The long-term ones are the alliance system, militarism, nationalism and imperialism, and the short-term trigger is the assassination at Sarajevo followed by the July Crisis. The July Crisis is where it escalates: Germany's blank cheque to Austria-Hungary, Austria's ultimatum to Serbia, Russia mobilizing, and the German plan through Belgium pulling Britain in.

items.question: Now repeat it forever.
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): Classic prisoner's dilemma. Each prisoner does better by confessing no matter what the other one does, so they both confess, even though both staying quiet would leave them better off.

NATIVELY: The key idea is that confessing is a **dominant strategy**: it gives each prisoner a better outcome regardless of what the other does. If the other stays quiet, confessing means going free instead of serving time. If the other confesses, confessing means a lighter sentence than staying quiet would. So rational self-interest leads both to confess, and they land on an outcome that's worse for both than mutual silence. That gap between individual rationality and collective good is the dilemma.
items.answer: When the game is played over and over with no known end, the logic shifts. In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, confessing is dominant. But in a repeated game, each player's choice today can be punished or rewarded tomorrow, so cooperation can become rational. That's the idea behind tit-for-tat: start by cooperating, then copy whatever the other player did last round. It's forgiving enough to restore cooperation and tough enough to deter cheating, which is why repetition is what makes cooperation sustainable.

items.question: So remember, when demand is elastic and you raise the price, total revenue goes up, and that's exactly why the cart owner did it.
conversation: PROFESSOR: Okay, back to the coffee cart outside Benning Hall. Price goes from three dollars to three sixty.
PROFESSOR: Sales drop from five hundred cups a day to four hundred, and with our midpoint formula that's an elasticity of one point two two.
PROFESSOR: So demand is elastic over that range.
items.answer: The lecturer's claim is actually backwards. When demand is elastic, a price increase **lowers** total revenue, not raises it. Here the cart went from $3.00 × 500 = $1,500 a day to $3.60 × 400 = $1,440, so revenue fell by $60. The rule is: elastic demand, price up, revenue down. Inelastic demand, price up, revenue up. So the cart owner's price hike cost them money, which is the opposite of what was just said.

items.question: But a lot of historians now call that the Westphalian myth. If you actually read the treaties, they say surprisingly little about sovereignty.
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): So the Peace of Westphalia, 1648, ends the Thirty Years' War, and it's usually taught as the moment the modern system of sovereign states is born.

NATIVELY: The Peace of Westphalia is actually a pair of treaties signed in 1648 at Münster and Osnabrück, and together they ended both the Thirty Years' War in the Empire and the Eighty Years' War between Spain and the Dutch Republic. What made it a turning point is that it recognized the territorial sovereignty of the many states within the Holy Roman Empire, giving each prince authority over religion and internal affairs, and it treated the Empire's constituent states as actors in their own right rather than through the Emperor alone. So the "birth of the sovereign state system" reading is a useful shorthand, though historians debate how much it was a clean break versus a formalizing of arrangements that had been developing for a while.
items.answer: That's the revisionist reading, and it's worth taking seriously. The treaties are mostly about specific grievances: which territories changed hands, confessional rights, compensation for the Palatinate, the imperial courts. The word "sovereignty" in the modern sense barely appears, and the Empire's princes still owed allegiance to the Emperor. What the treaties did do is grant the imperial estates the right to make alliances and conduct their own foreign policy, which later scholars read back as sovereignty. So the myth isn't that 1648 mattered, it's that it created a system of equal sovereign states in one stroke. The label is a nineteenth and twentieth century projection onto a settlement that was really about ending a specific war.
